bio.en: Julie Zhuo spent 13 years at Facebook, rising from an individual-contributor designer to VP of Product Design, and is the bestselling author of The Making of a Manager.
bio.zh: 朱莉·卓（Julie Zhuo）在 Facebook 工作了 13 年，从一线设计师成长为产品设计副总裁，并著有畅销书《创作者之路》（The Making of a Manager）。

summary.en: In Lenny's very first episode, Julie shares hard-won career advice, from overcoming imposter syndrome to running effective product review meetings. She discusses what great design hiring and feedback look like, and how her immigrant background shaped her relentless work ethic. The conversation is a foundational primer on product leadership and personal growth.

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. It is a pleasure to be here. I think it's going to be a super fun conversation.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。很高兴能来参加节目。我觉得这会是一次非常有趣的对谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For listeners who maybe aren't familiar with you and your career, could you just kind of briefly walk us through your journey in design and then a little bit about what you're up to these days?
turns.zh: 对于可能不熟悉你和你的职业生涯的听众，你能否简要介绍一下你在设计领域的历程，以及你目前的动态？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Okay. So, let's see. I am a first generation immigrant to the United States, and so, with Asian parents, there were really only three options that I had for a career. From the time I was six years old, I was told I could either be a doctor, a lawyer, or an engineer. Nothing else was really in the realm of possibilities. Unfortunately, I was really scared of blood, so I couldn't be a doctor, and I only liked reading fiction growing up, so I was like, "Never really be a lawyer." So, I was always like, "Okay, right, this engineering thing," but actually, it was during middle school and high school that I discovered what I love to do is drawing and in particular digital art, and the reason for that is because I actually have a very shaky hands, and so, whenever I draw a line, it never looks good, I have to erase it, start over, and so, by the time the art was done, it was a mess. It was like here's like 20,000 eraser remarks. (00:03:45): But when I discovered MS Paint, and I kid you not, that was my very first design application, I was like, "Oh my gosh, I can draw a line, and even if it looks crummy," which it always does because you have to use a mouse in those early days, "I can just Ctrl+Z, it goes away, and just keep trying over and over again. No one ever has to know how often I tried to get to this to be what I wanted." And so, MS Paint became PaintShop Pro, and then one summer I finagled my way into a pirated copy of Photoshop because I couldn't actually afford real Photoshop, and I was off to the races in my digital art career. (00:04:16): It was actually through digital art that I realized, "Okay, I've actually amassed all this collection of art. What should I do?" And I was like, "Well, let me go and actually build a website. All these artists that I admire on the internet did that. So, I'm going to learn how to write HTML and put together a website," and that's essentially what I did on the side in my middle and high school years. (00:04:34): So, that's kind of how I got into design, but I didn't know it was design because I really still thought of myself as an artist, and I thought that the only thing I could be was an engineer, but I went in and studied computer science in college. Right? I always had this vision, "Okay, if I like building websites, maybe computer engineering is the closest thing to that," and I had this idea that maybe I could go work for one of these big tech companies, and after I took a class my senior year, that taught me what is Silicon Valley, what is entrepreneurship. By the way, here's all these stories of two people in a garage, and then they went and built something big, and I totally just was so into that. I was like, "All right, I do not want to work for a big company. I want to figure out if I can do this startup thing and make something small into something big." (00:05:17): I just happened to be very lucky at the time. There was a startup down the street from my university. It's a product I had been using for two or three years. It was Facebook. It was still a high school and college social networking product at the time, 8 million users. They were doing a lot of recruitment at Stanford, and so, that's how I decided to go and join for an internship, and on my first day I remember my mentor, Ruchi, she said, "What kind of engineering do you like to do?" And I was like, "The stuff that people see, of course. I want to be able to..." The stuff that I'd always done. Right? And she goes, "Oh, I see. You should go sit next to the designers," and that was the first time I heard that design was a profession, that it was actually a job. It was a thing that people did. (00:05:55): Back in those days, all of the design team was technical. So, we were both the front-end engineers as well as the designers, but I felt like I'd found my tribe. I had found people who kind of had always been passionate about this thing that I didn't really realize was a job. And so, I realized though as well that I had a lot to learn about design. I was never really formally trained in it. Right? I'd only ever designed for myself for me to express my creative, artistic side, so there was a lot in those first three years. I would think of my time at Facebook as chapter one, learn how to be a designer, learn about usability, learn about the actual language, nomenclature of design, learn how to think about the user as somebody separate than just me and my own work. (00:06:36): Then, because Facebook was always scaling, I got the opportunity to eventually manage a team of designers. Totally unprepared for that, no idea what I was doing, kind of jumped in, and just started to manage, but there was a huge amount of learning around recruiting, process, what even is good design, what is the way that we want to design at this company in our team, and so, tons of learnings there. The third chapter is just sort thinking about scale. Right? Learning how to scale in management, learning how to build a wide diversity of products, learning more about strategy, and how design fits into working with all of these other disciplines to build something great. So, that's kind of how I think about my time at Facebook and the various chapters. (00:07:16): The latest chapter is eventually I left Facebook about two years ago and now I am a startup founder. So, it's something that I've always wanted to do. So, go back to that, the early phases of figuring out how to build something from zero to one, and I'm working on a product and product analytics. I'm really passionate about the idea of making data accessible about... I've seen the power firsthand from working at Facebook of what data can do to help us make better products, especially for people at scale, to help us reduce the bias in our intuitions, and how we think about what is the way that we should prioritize, and I'm really passionate about the idea of making that such that every single company, every single business in the world can properly use data, know how to interpret it correctly, know how to use it to influence roadmap strategy and prioritization decisions, and make better decisions as a result.
turns.zh:
好的。让我想想。我是美国第一代移民，父母都是亚洲人，所以我能选择的职业道路只有三个。从六岁起，我就被告知可以成为医生、律师或工程师，其他选择根本不被考虑。遗憾的是，我特别害怕血，所以当不了医生；而我从小就喜欢读小说，也从没想过当律师。所以我最后只能选了工程学。不过在初中和高中时期，我发现自己真正热爱的是绘画，尤其是数字艺术。这是因为我的手很不稳，每次画线都不理想，总要擦掉重来，一幅作品最后总是一团糟，满是修正痕迹。（00:03:45）但当我发现MS Paint这款软件时——说真的，那是我人生第一个设计应用——我兴奋极了："天哪，我终于能画直线了！即使画得丑也能用Ctrl+Z撤销，不断重来！没人会知道我费了多少功夫才能达到理想效果。"后来MS Paint升级为PaintShop Pro，某个夏天我甚至破解了Photoshop的盗版软件——毕竟正版太贵了——从此开启了我的数字艺术之旅。（00:04:16）通过数字艺术，我意识到："我积累了这么多作品，该怎么展示呢？"于是我决定建个网站，模仿网上那些艺术家。我学会了HTML编程，亲手搭建网站，这就是我初高中时代的业余爱好。

（00:04:34）这就是我进入设计领域的契机，但当时我并不认为自己是设计师，因为我始终认为自己是艺术家，只想当工程师。结果大学我却选择了计算机科学专业。某节课上，我了解到硅谷和创业精神，特别是那些车库创业故事，瞬间被深深吸引："好吧，我不想在大公司工作，想看看能否从零到一打造一家小公司。"

（00:05:17）当时运气特别好。大学附近正好有家创业公司，产品叫Facebook。当时还是高中和大学社交平台，用户8百万。他们在斯坦福招人，于是我去实习。第一天导师鲁奇问："你喜欢哪种工程？"我回答："当然是用户能看到的部分啊。"她说："那你应该去设计组。"那是我第一次意识到设计才是我的归宿。
职业生涯中，我曾误以为设计只是一份工作，是人们为了谋生而做的事。（00:05:55）：那时设计团队都是技术人员，所以我们既是前端工程师，也是设计师。但我突然意识到，自己找到了志同道合的伙伴——那些和我一样，对这个行业充满热情的人。我也意识到自己在设计方面还有很多需要学习的地方。毕竟我从未接受过正式培训。当时我只为自己设计，用来展现自己的创造力和艺术才华。所以，在Facebook的头三年里，我收获颇丰。我把这段经历视为第一章——学习如何成为一名设计师，掌握可用性原则，熟悉设计的专业术语，学会如何将用户视为独立个体，而非仅是自我表达的工具。

（00:06:36）：随着Facebook不断扩张，我有机会管理设计团队。虽然毫无准备，手忙脚乱，但通过不断摸索，我逐渐掌握了招聘、流程管理等技能，深刻理解了优秀设计的标准，以及团队设计理念。第三章主要探索规模化管理——如何在管理中实现扩展，如何开发多样化产品，深化战略思维，并协调各专业领域共同打造卓越成果。

（00:07:16）：最近两年离开Facebook后，我成为了一名初创公司创始人。这一阶段让我重返初心——从零到一打造产品。目前我专注于产品开发和数据分析，致力于让数据更易于理解。我深知数据在产品优化中的价值，尤其是在大规模场景下能减少直觉偏差，指导优先级决策。我希望每个企业都能合理运用数据，正确解读分析结果，优化路线图策略与决策流程，从而做出更明智的决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like that, this idea that you're working on has such intense founder market fit, and I can't wait to hear more about it when you're ready to kind of go deeper and for people to use it. But going back to your time at Facebook, you kind of made it sound like you just kind of like, "I joined as a designer, figured out design, became a manager," and then somehow you became VP of design, and it sounded too easy. That's an insane trajectory for someone to follow. Do you have any thoughts or advice on what contributed to your success rising through the ranks that quickly for folks that are kind of just early in their career maybe?
turns.zh: 我觉得就是这样，你正在开发的这个项目与创始人市场的契合度实在太高了。等你准备好深入探讨并让用户实际使用时，我迫不及待想听听更多细节。但说回你在Facebook的经历，你说得好像自己只是个设计师，学会了设计，就当了经理，然后不知怎么就当上了设计副总裁，听起来太容易了。这对大多数人来说，尤其是刚入行的新人来说，简直难以企及。你有没有什么心得或建议，能帮助那些在职业生涯早期的人更快地晋升？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Absolutely, and I want to make it really clear. I always say that the first seven or eight years that I was at Facebook, every single week, I felt like an imposter. I had no idea really what I was doing. The constant refrain in my head is like, "Well, do you really deserve to be here? Do you really know what's happening? You're not really prepared for this job. You've never done this before. What right do you have to be put in this situation and get to do what you do?" Right? And that was really a constant refrain in my head. (00:09:03): But looking back, I think it probably took me about, yeah, seven or eight years till I became a little bit more comfortable with that, and after seven or eight years, I could look back, I could see all of the things that I got to work on, I could see all the ways that I had grown and learned in that experience, and something clicked for me where I realized it's kind of two sides of the same coin. Right? Being in an uncomfortable situation, being in a position where you feel like, Hey, do I really know how to do this? I've not prepared for it is kind of coin sides with the fastest and most intense periods of growth in one's career. And I started to realize, well, maybe it's not so much of a bad thing. Right? Maybe if I am constantly putting myself in a situation where I haven't seen this problem before, that's also what's going to push me to grow and learn. Right? (00:09:47): And so, yes, you asked for specific advice. I think there's two things. The first is, well, I was lucky. I was in the right place at the right time. I was at a company that was scaling, and when you're at a company that grows, there's always a lot more opportunity to then be able to try something new, right, to raise your hand, to volunteer for things to be just thrown into because somebody has to do it because it's a growing company and a lot of other people. So, the first piece of advice I have would be like if you want those types of opportunities, sometimes you just have to be at a smaller place and you have to be at a place that is going through that rate of growth. The second thing is embrace the fact that it's okay to be in a position where maybe you don't know what to do, you haven't been trained for. Right? It does coincide with that intense learning. Maybe approach it with that sense of curiosity and that sense of yes, it's hard, yes, I might be an imposter and I might feel that way for a while, but this is also what's going to help me get there. It's going to be what forces me to do the work, and in that process, learn and become better.
turns.zh: 当然，我想先明确一点。我常说，在Facebook的前七八年里，每周我都觉得自己是个冒牌货。我完全不知道自己在做什么。脑子里不断回荡着这样的声音：“你真的配得上在这里吗？你真的了解正在发生什么吗？你根本没准备好这份工作。你以前从未做过这类事。你有什么资格被置于这种境地，从事现在的工作？” 对吧？这真的成了我脑海里挥之不去的念头。（00:09:03）但回首往事，我大概花了七八年时间才稍微适应这种状态。七八年后，我回首往事，能看到自己参与过的所有项目，看到自己在那段经历中成长和学习的痕迹，然后突然意识到，这两者其实是同一枚硬币的两面。对吧？身处不舒适的境地，觉得自己“真的不知道怎么做这件事？”“我根本没准备好”，正是职业生涯中成长最快、最激烈的时期。我开始意识到，或许这未必是件坏事。对吧？或许不断把自己置于未曾遇到过的问题中，这恰恰能推动我成长和学习。（00:09:47）所以，是的，你问具体建议。我觉得有两点：第一，我很幸运。当时我在正确的时间出现在正确的地方。我所在的公司正在扩张，成长型公司总有更多机会去尝试新事物——比如主动请缨，主动参与未经授权的项目，因为公司需要人手，因为它在快速发展。所以我的第一个建议是，如果你想获得这些机会，有时你就得去小公司，得去经历快速成长的公司。第二，要接受这样一个事实：有时你可能不知道该做什么，缺乏相关培训。对吧？但这恰恰与高强度学习相契合。或许你可以带着好奇心去面对，带着“这很难，我可能会觉得自己是个冒牌货，可能会有段时间这样，但这也会帮助我成长”的心态。正是这种挑战，驱使你投入工作，学习并提升自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's amazing to hear that you had imposter syndrome for such a long period of time and you basically ran design for the Facebook app. Right? And so, it's kind of an empowering, inspiring insight that someone at your level went through that for so long and made it through that. Do you have any other advice or thoughts on just for folks that are going through that? Because I had that too for a number of years, just like, "What the hell am I doing here? People are going to see I don't really know what I'm doing, and it's all going to crumble as soon as I make my next mistake." Do you have any other advice there for folks going through that themselves?
turns.zh: 听说你长期受困于冒名顶替综合症，却依然能负责Facebook应用的设计工作，这真是令人惊叹。是吧？所以，看到你这种级别的人能克服这种心理障碍，取得成功，真是鼓舞人心、振奋士气的。对于那些正在经历同样困境的人，你有什么建议或心得吗？因为我自己也曾深受其扰多年——总觉得“我到底在这里干什么？别人会发现我根本不知道自己在做什么，只要我再犯一个错，一切就都会崩塌。”对于那些正经历类似心理斗争的人，你有什么实用的应对建议吗？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I think just exactly what you said, Lenny, right? I think so much of it that helped me was realizing that everyone feels this way to some extent, and that's also why I always want to talk about that, right, because I feel like sometimes you can see from the outside. You're like, "Oh, this person has this title. They have this position. They have these responsibilities. Clearly, they've made it. They know what they're doing." But that's never the case, and I mean, logically let's think about it. Right? If you're going to do anything new for the first time, how are you ever going to feel totally comfortable, totally prepared? Every time, there's something new that you hadn't encountered before, it's always going to be a little bit rough. You're never going to feel perfectly at ease. (00:11:50): It's only upon doing something multiple times that you start to see the patterns, you start to realize, "Okay, it's going to be all right." And even now the people that I talk to, the people I really look up to, the people who I think are role models and mentors for me, I mean, they regularly also share with me that it's the same. It's like they still encounter things that are unprecedented. Right? And if we work in tech, I mean the rate of change, the rate of the industry and companies and kind of these new experiences that we have, that never goes away. Right? That's just par for the course. And so, I think that feeling always exists. (00:12:24): I think that what I have learned is that there are better tools in your toolkit for dealing with it. One of them is of course me just reminding myself that if I feel uncomfortable, it's okay. Other people feel that way too. Everyone does. It's totally natural, but then to also find other pieces in that toolkit. Right? One is I am much better at asking for help now than I was earlier in my career. I used to actually just try and hold it all in. I was like, "Hey, I better fake it until I make it. If everyone thinks that maybe I'm coming to a table like I know it, then I can fool them." And now I realize I was really just, I was preventing myself from being able to get that support and that empathy and that camaraderie and that advice that would've helped me actually grow faster and maybe with a little bit less pain in the process. (00:13:09): And so, one of the things I learned is it's okay to ask for help. It's okay to reach out to people who both may be going through the same things you're going or maybe are step or two ahead of you in the journey, right, who have actually gone through that and have lived to tell the tale and can tell you it's going to be okay because often that's just what you need. You just need people to tell you, "It's going to be fine. You're fine. You're good. You've got this." And that's so meaningful, right, whenever we sometimes feel down about ourselves. So, that's another, I would say tool in the toolkit, right, asking for help, finding groups of support. (00:13:39): And then I think the third is it's also okay to just be vulnerable and just talk to people about it. Right? I found that some of the most meaningful conversations I had, whether with people like managers or whether with my own reports is when we can be much more open about what it is that we find hard, what are we struggling with, and in that way, you actually form deeper connections and people are more able to help out. Right? We can spread the load a little bit. We can put our heads together and brainstorm a better way to solve the problem, and I find that too, even as the head of a department, right, or a founder, it's like I'm not going to solve everything myself. I'm never going to have all the answers. Sometimes by just sharing what the problem is, by sharing the load, we're all going to collectively come up with a better solution.
turns.zh:
我觉得你说得太对了，伦尼！我深有同感——帮助我最多的就是意识到，每个人或多或少都会有这种感受。这也是我总想聊起这个话题的原因，因为有时你从外界看别人时，会觉得“哦，这个人头衔显赫，职位重要，责任重大。显然他们已经成功了，什么都懂。”但事实绝非如此。试想一下，当你第一次尝试新事物时，怎么可能从一开始就感到游刃有余、准备充分呢？每次面对未知，总会遇到些小挫折，永远无法做到完全游刃有余。（00:11:50）只有在多次实践后，你才会逐渐发现规律，意识到“其实一切都会好起来的”。即便现在，我与那些我敬仰、视为榜样和导师的人交流时，他们也坦言仍会遇到前所未有的挑战。毕竟我们身处科技行业，行业变革、公司发展以及新体验的速度从未停歇。这就是常态，所以这种不安感始终存在。

（00:12:24）我领悟到，应对这种情绪有更好的方法。其中之一就是提醒自己：感到不安是正常的，其他人也一样。这完全自然。但更重要的是，要学会寻求帮助。早期职业生涯时，我总试图独自面对，伪装成无所不能的样子。但现在我意识到，这样只会阻碍自己获得支持、同理心、友谊和建议，这些本可以帮助我更快成长，减少痛苦。

（00:13:09）所以，学会求助很重要。可以向正在经历相同挑战，或比你领先一步的人寻求帮助，他们经历过低谷，知道如何安慰你。这正是你需要的——有人告诉你“会好起来的，你很棒，别担心。” 这对自我怀疑时极具意义。

（00:13:39）第三点是坦诚脆弱，勇于倾诉。我发现，与上司或下属最有意义的对话，就是坦诚分享挑战与困境。这样能建立更深厚的连接，激发集体智慧。我作为部门负责人，深有体会——团队协作能分担压力，共同破解难题。
创始人啊，我又不是要独自解决所有问题。我永远不可能知晓所有答案。有时候，只要把问题说出来，共同分担压力，大家就能集思广益，找到更好的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. It's so simple and so effective. Reminds me of advice a coach once told me that when you're in a new role, you are an imposter. You're doing something you've never done before and that's normal and don't feel like that's unusual. So, speaking of being uncomfortable and being vulnerable and doing hard things, you now have a startup that you've started and I'm curious. What's kind of different from the experience of being a leader at a Meta versus being a founder, especially things that maybe are surprising, good or bad?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个建议。它既简单又实用。这让我想起一位教练曾对我说的话：当你身处新角色时，你就是个冒牌货。你正在做从未做过的事情，这很正常，不必觉得自己格格不入。说到克服不适、展现脆弱、挑战难题，你现在创办了一家初创公司，我很好奇。与在Meta担任领导者相比，身为创始人有何不同之处？尤其是那些可能令人惊讶的经验教训，无论是积极的还是消极的。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I will say it is definitely a very humbling experience, but it's also exactly the journey that I wanted, and a lot of it is just going back to kind of this like base layer. When you're at a large company, a lot is taken care of for you. Right? If I have a question about, I don't know, finance or how to deal with a people situation, they're experts. There's experts in every single field, and I just go and reach out to them and talk to them and kind of handle that and help me. But when you get back to it, it's like, okay. In the beginning, it was myself and my founder, Chandra. It's just the two of us, and it was like all sorts of stuff that it was like talk about being an imposter. It's setting up, figuring out taxes, or just figuring out how to incorporate, or just thousand little decisions, right, a thousand little things that were new and different. (00:15:34): So, there's a huge amount of learning. There's a huge amount of just having to do it all yourself and realizing in a lot of ways just how many things you're bad at, or don't really like to do and that because you don't like to do them, it's hard to get them done. Right? So, it's humbling that way of just helping you realize these things about who you are. (00:15:52): I think the other thing is for me, it's going back to the idea of being much more focused on doing, working with people who are at different stages in their career. When I was leading design for let's say the last five or seven years, right, I was often directly managing senior people, either senior designers or managers or directors and so forth, and going back to working with folks at various stages, including new grads, early career folks, it was actually both me realizing I had to kind of really change a lot of how I manage, so it was, again, also very humbling in that respect. I had to change a lot of what good management looks like in that context which was different from a lot of the habits that I had built up, but it was also so rewarding. I realized I actually really love working with people who are in that early phase of their careers. It's totally different, and what they need and how to best support them is really different than what you would do with a director or very senior person, but it's also just a whole lot of fun. (00:16:50): So, that was something that is really new, and then of course, so much of it is again putting that IC hat back on, right, and it's been years since I've actually sat down and designed. Often as a manager, the thing I develop is I develop my eye, but not my hand. So, I learned to be a good critiquer of design, but actually because I stop practicing design, I'm definitely, the limits of what I can actually make and what I can produce myself become really evident. Right? And so, again, back in this new company setting, well, I have to put on a bit of that IC hat. I have to learn how to be kind of an ICPM learn how to be an IC designer, realize that there's so much that I'm actually really bad at as well and in that way, but develop and grow some of my muscles and those skills again.
turns.zh:
我得说，这绝对是一次令人谦卑的经历，但这也正是我想要的旅程。很多时候，我不过是在回归到某种基础层面。当你在大公司工作时，很多事情都有人替你处理。对吧？如果我遇到财务问题或人际关系难题，他们都是专家。每个领域都有专家，我只需主动联系他们交流，解决问题。但当你独自面对时，一切都得自己操办。从一开始，只有我和创始人钱德拉。所有事情都要亲力亲为——从谈论冒名顶替综合症，到设立公司、处理税务、注册公司，再到数千个新奇而不同的小决策。（00:15:34）：因此，学习的量非常大。你必须亲力亲为，意识到自己在很多方面做得很糟糕，或者不喜欢做的事情。正因为不喜欢做这些事，就很难完成它们。所以，这种谦卑感能让你认清自己，认识到自己的不足。
（00:15:52）：对我来说，另一个收获是回归到专注行动的理念，与处于不同职业阶段的人合作。比如过去五到七年，我负责设计工作，经常直接管理资深设计师、经理或总监等人员。现在回到与不同阶段的人共事，包括应届生、初入职场者，我意识到自己必须彻底改变管理方式。这在某种程度上也令人谦卑，因为我需要调整管理思路，突破既有习惯，但收获满满。我发现自己其实非常喜欢与初入职场者合作。这完全不同，他们的需求和支持方式与高管或资深人士截然不同，但也乐趣无穷。
（00:16:50）：这对我来说是全新的体验。当然，重拾设计师身份也很重要。多年来，我作为管理者培养了审美眼光，但失去了动手能力。现在我必须重新拿起画笔，学习如何成为一名合格的IC设计师，意识到自己在很多方面仍有欠缺。但通过不断学习和实践，我得以重塑技能，成长为更全面的从业者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The first point you made about having to do everything again, I remember the reverse of that when we sold our startup. I was so happy just to like, "Okay, here's a one goal we're going to focus on. We don't have to think about everything in the company all the time. I'm just going to hit this one goal, this one product. It's going to be so, so much easier." And that was really fun for a while, and then gets itchy and hard again, and you kind of want to have more responsibility and more challenge.
turns.zh: 你提到的第一点——不得不把所有事情重新做一遍。我记得我们出售初创公司时，也有过相反的经历。当时我特别开心，就想：“好吧，现在我们只需专注于一个目标，不必整天操心公司里的大小事务。我只要专注于这个目标、这款产品，事情就会简单得多。”那段时光确实很愉快，但后来又会变得焦虑和困难起来，你总想承担更多责任，迎接更大的挑战。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: It's fun though. I am really enjoying it.
turns.zh: 不过这也很有趣。我现在真的很享受这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah. I want to transition a little bit to talking about your writing and writing in general. I think I mentioned that your newsletter, The Looking Glass, inspired my writing in a big way. I basically modeled your newsletter and focused it on growth and product. That was the idea. Let me just do what Julie's doing and I'll do it around a different vertical. And so, first of all, I just want to thank you for all the writing that you've done over the years because it was really impactful to me. And so, first of all, thank you for doing that.
turns.zh: 哦，对了。我想稍微转换话题，聊聊你的写作和写作这件事。我之前提过，你的《镜报》（The Looking Glass）对我写作影响很大。我基本上是模仿你的新闻通讯，专注于增长和产品。这就是我的思路。我想，既然朱莉（Julie）能做到，那我也能在不同领域尝试。所以首先，我要感谢你这些年来的写作，它对我影响深远。真的很感谢你。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Oh, thank you for sharing that. It's really meaningful for me to hear as well.
turns.zh: 哦，谢谢你分享这些。听你这么说，我也深有感触。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I still go back to a lot of your writing, even though I know you've slowed down the focus on the startup which makes a lot of sense, and we'll chat a little bit about that. But I'm curious, what got you to start the writing, and broadly, what impact have you seen it have on your career and just anything in life?
turns.zh: 虽然我知道你现在把精力转向了初创公司，这很明智，我们稍后再聊这个。但我很好奇，你最初为什么开始写作？从更广泛的角度看，你的写作对你的职业生涯和生活有什么影响？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: What actually started me on this writing journey was a piece of feedback I got during a performance review cycle, and I remember I was talking to my manager and he shared that, "Hey, one of the pieces of something you should work on, an area of growth is that you have a lot of really great ideas, and you're always really engaged whenever discussions happen in a small forum, one on one, or there's like two or three people in the room, but whenever there's a large room, we're talking about seven people, 10 people, 15 people, you're just sort of quiet and you're not really telling your perspective. You're not really contributing to these larger conversations, and that's something for you to think about and work on." (00:19:19): It was really good feedback because I absolutely felt it. I definitely felt that barrier of speaking up in a large room. I think the fear could be summarized as I don't want to look stupid in front of a lot of people. And so, I had all these barriers. I was like, "Okay, am I sure that what I'm going to say, what comes out of my mouth is absolutely brilliant?" And that was really just this emotion that was getting in the way, and I was like, "Okay, I really want to work on this. I want to figure out how to get that to be less and less of a friction for me." (00:19:47): And so, it was around I think the January timeframe. Right? So, when the new year came, I was like, "Okay, here's an idea. What if I just did something," that at the time seemed really scary to me which was put my opinion out there on the internet and just do it, just do it for a year. Okay? My goal was post one thing every single week. It seemed terrifying. Right? I'm not sure what people are going to say. Again, maybe all my ideas are stupid, but I just want to get better at doing that, and hopefully, through that year, get more comfortable with that. (00:20:18): So, that's how this whole writing thing began. It came with this kind of New Year's resolution of just 52 times, I was going to click publish on something, some opinion piece. And I was like, "It doesn't have to even be..." It doesn't even matter what the opinion is. Just put something out there and just expose yourself a little bit in that manner. So, that's what I did, and I tried to not have any goals around, well, maybe people will read it, maybe it'll be considered high quality. Those are all just, again, additional barriers that I was putting that would make me even harder for me. The only goal was to hit the publish button. (00:20:49): And so, the first couple weeks were actually quite excruciating. I remember I just spent hours on this piece and I just kept editing it, and I was like, "I don't know if this is any good? Should I actually publish it?" And so forth, but eventually, I did it. Right? And again, little by little, it started to just become easier as anything does when it's done a lot. So, by week 10, by week 15, I had gotten into a bit of a cadence, and I realized something that was having an impact on my work. I realized that it became much more clarifying for me to have that space to be able to write, and it almost became a kind of self-therapy because through the week I would have all these thoughts running around my head, things I wanted to get better at, pieces of product that I was mulling on, and the act of writing allowed me some quiet time to just sit down and try and organize those different threads of thoughts. (00:21:40): I approach my writing then and I still do now as letters to myself. This is the framework. This is the advice that I need to give myself that I need to go and really do better, and that is what my writing became for me, and it was hugely helpful for clarifying my train of thought. It was hugely helpful for me to then be able to do a better job of expressing myself, and by the end of that year, I saw a huge difference in my ability then in large meetings to speak up and to become more comfortable. (00:22:11): But even after that year, because I had seen all of these advantages in what it did for my clarity of thinking, and I just decided to continue, and it became also a really, I think, a wonderful side effect that other people started to resonate with the writing. They were like, "Oh, this is actually helpful for me, or I was feeling the same thing, or this gave me a little bit of additional structure to think about the problem," and that was also extremely motivating, but I will say that what I think helped me continue the writing habit is I always did it for me. I always did it because I felt that there was a lot that I had to gain from it, and it's been obviously a wonderful experience to connect with readers and other people in the community about it. It definitely made me feel less alone. It definitely confirmed a lot of the ideas that I had about is this the right way to think about something. It led to a lot of really rich discussion with my colleagues and with people who just emailed or responded about the writing. So, that was a wonderful side benefit as well. But yeah, I really credit my ability to think better through the process and the practice of writing.
turns.zh:
真正促使我踏上写作之路的，是一次绩效评估期间收到的反馈。我记得当时和经理交谈时，他指出：“嘿，有一点你需要改进——你有很多很棒的想法，每当在小型论坛、一对一交流或三四个人参与的场合讨论时，总能积极发言。但当面对七人、十人、十五人这样的大群体时，你就变得沉默寡言，很少参与大型对话。这值得你反思并努力改进。”  (00:19:19)  
这确实是很有价值的反馈，因为我深有同感。我确实能感受到在大群体发言时的障碍。恐惧可能归结为不想在众人面前出丑。种种心理因素让我纠结：“我确定自己要说的话一定很棒吗？”这种自我怀疑成了最大的阻碍。于是，我决定尝试新方法：在新年伊始，我制定了一个目标——每周发布一篇文章。 (00:19:47)  
回想起来，整个写作之旅始于一月份。新年伊始，我想：“何不试试看？”将个人观点公之于众，坚持一年。这看似可怕，但我决心克服恐惧，逐步提升表达能力。 (00:20:18)  
最初的几周异常煎熬。记得我花数小时润色文章，犹豫不决：“这篇文章真的好吗？要不要发布？”但最终还是按下了发布键。随着练习次数增加，写作变得越来越自然。 (00:20:49)  
到第10周、第15周时，我形成了固定的写作节奏。发现写作不仅能理清思路，更像是一种自我疗愈。每周脑海中涌现的想法、待改进的产品、深思熟虑的决策，都能在写作中得到梳理。 (00:21:40)  
至今，我仍以写信自勉的心态对待写作。这就是框架，也是我要给自己的忠告。
于是我需要去真正做得更好，而写作对我来说就成了实现这一目标的途径。它极大地帮助我理清了思路，也让我能更流畅地表达自己。到那年年底，我在大型会议上发言时明显感觉到自己比之前自信多了，也更从容自如了。（00:22:11）但即便那一年结束后，我依然坚持了下来——因为我深知写作对思维清晰度的诸多益处，于是决定继续坚持。令人欣喜的是，其他读者也开始与我的文字产生共鸣。他们会说：“哦，这对我也很有帮助！”或者“我也有同样的感受！”这给了我极大的动力。不过我认为真正让我能坚持写作的关键在于，我始终是为了自己而写。我写作是因为深知自己能从中收获良多。而与读者及社区成员交流心得，更是难得的体验。这让我不再感到孤单，也验证了许多自己关于思考方式的假设。与同事、读者们就文章展开的深入讨论，更是收获满满。所以，我要归功于写作过程和实践所带来的思维提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a cool story. I love that it was kind of driven by a manager, but kind of led to so many externalities. One thing I wanted to ask you is how did you find time to this writing? People always want to write and very few people do or find time to. How did you actually make the time and keep that up?
turns.zh: 太棒了，这个故事太酷了。我很喜欢它最初是由一位经理推动的，但最终却引发了诸多外部效应。我想问你的是，您是如何抽出时间来写作的？人们总是想写作，但真正能坚持下来的人却寥寥无几。您是如何挤出时间并坚持下去的？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: So, I actually had this practice of writing even before I did this more publicly with a blog, and it was because I harbored this dream back when I was a teenager and well into my college years of one day writing the next great American novel. So, I wrote a lot of fiction and I wrote a lot of... I have four unpublished novels just collecting dust. They're not very good. I can say that now with a lot more objectivity. (00:23:52): But I did that, and I would participate in this program called NaNoWriMo every year which later I was fortunate enough to be on the board for a number of years. But what NaNoWriMo was is this idea of... It Stands for National Novel Writing Month in November. So, it's exactly what it sounds like. In the month of November, the goal is to write 50,000-word novel in 30 days, and the whole purpose and the whole point of NaNoWriMo, and again, I did it for a number of years in my early twenties, it's all about just getting the words out. Right? It's not about, hey, is every paragraph, is every sentence pristine, or do you have the right beginning, middle, end. It was like no. It was like you're going to write a novel every single day. You need to write 1,667 words, and you just do that over 30 days, you'll have 50,000 words. (00:24:37): The whole premise was, yeah, no, those 50,000 words, they're definitely going to be junk. They're not going to be really good. But at the end you'll have something that you can then edit and then you can shape and you refine. Right? And the hardest part is just getting started. It's just getting past the blank screen and the first page. (00:24:55): And so, because I'd gone through that experience, I had really internalized that writing for me is just get the words out. It is just about the sit your butt in the seat and just do it, get the word count goal out or get a time goal. I actually like word count goal even better than time goal because sometimes you can spend 30 minutes and then still just produce a sentence, and so, that was always how I approached my writing. I was like, "All right, I'm going to sit my butt down. I'm going to write for 30 or 45 minutes, but it's going to be, whatever, like 250 words. It's going to be 500 words. It's going to be this number of words." And that just gave me the discipline to just get it out and then think about revising, think about quality, think about all that later. (00:25:32): And when I got into writing my book, that was exactly how I approached the first draft. I was like, "Okay, I'm going to divide up. It needs to be 60 or 70,000 words. I have like a year. I'm going to divide it up into the number of days and weeks." And I think what it came down to for me was five nights a week, I needed to write 500 words each day, and I eventually got that down to, it was like 30 or 45 minutes. I mean, some days, a little longer, other days, a little shorter, but it was about that, and I just kept that weekly goal up until the book was written.
turns.zh: 其实我写作的习惯早在公开写博客之前就养成了。那时我还是个青少年和大学生，怀揣着未来能写出下一部美国伟大小说的梦想。因此，我写了许多小说，但大部分都未能发表，如今看来确实不算出色。（00:23:52）不过我一直坚持，每年都会参加“全国小说写作月”（NaNoWriMo）活动，还很幸运地在其中担任过多年董事会成员。NaNoWriMo的理念很简单——11月份用30天写出5万字小说。重点不在于每段每句是否完美，也不必追求开头、中间、结尾的完美结构。关键在于坚持日更。（00:24:37）最初的设定是：这5万字肯定是草稿，质量不高。但最终你会得到初稿，通过润色完善。最难的部分就是开始动笔，克服空白屏幕的恐惧。（00:24:55）基于这样的经验，我深信写作就是把字写出来。关键在于坐下来行动，完成字数目标或时间目标。我甚至更偏爱字数目标，因为有时30分钟只写出一句话。写作时我会定个时间目标，比如30或45分钟，写250、500字。这让我养成自律习惯，先输出再追求质量。（00:25:32）写书时，我也采用了同样的方法。分解目标：6万到7万字，一年时间，每周分摊任务。我坚持每周五晚写500字，最终缩短到30到45分钟。偶尔会多写，偶尔少写，但始终保持每周目标，直到完成初稿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of the book, I definitely wanted to chat about that briefly. Did you always know you wanted to write a book or is this kind of a thing that emerged from people just asking you the same questions again and again, and then similarly, what impact have you seen from that book, which I own many copies and have gifted many copies?
turns.zh: 说到那本书，我确实想简单聊聊。您是从一开始就想写一本书，还是因为人们反复问同样的问题才萌生了这个想法？另外，您觉得那本书产生了什么影响？我自己就收藏了好几本，还送过不少给别人。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Thank you. I had this dream that I would write the great American novel. I still want to do that someday. One day, I really do want to sit down and hopefully write a fiction book. So, I always had that on my mind. I don't think I ever thought that I would write a non-fiction book. I never thought I would write a business book, right? That really came about organically, and it came about because I was writing this blog and I was publishing these letters to myself that I was again putting on the internet, and then occasionally, I would have publishers or various folks reach out and say, "Oh, this was a really great article. Have you ever thought about developing that into a book?" And my answer for the longest time was always like, "No, because I don't think I have the stamina to make this one topic into this huge thing. I don't think about myself as kind of like a career writer." Honestly, there wasn't necessarily anything that I felt that differentiated or maybe a unique angle. (00:27:03): I also felt that most books that I read, there was always a huge amount of research that went into it, and I was like, "I just..." I know this about myself. I don't love research, not great at it. I don't want to sit there and compile a bunch of stats and whatnot to make an argument. But one day, a publisher reached out and they were like, "You know, we had some ideas about the fact that you're writing really, especially the part about for new managers, your advice for new managers or for people new to leadership, it really seems like it strikes a chord for that particular audience, and we have some ideas. Why don't we get on the phone to discuss?" I took that call and actually really was... That call just did change my perspective because it gave me a particular angle on something that I felt was missing in the market. Right? (00:27:44): Again, most of the stuff that I'm writing, again, they're advice to myself, but I was brought back to when I first became a manager, and I went back, I went to the bookstore one day, I was looking for resources on what it means to manage and stuff that would help me become a better manager, and not a lot of it spoke to me because it seemed like most management books were written by CEOs who had been leading their company for years and years, or it was by management consultants who didn't really seem like they had been in the situation of just like, "Hey, I was an IC on the team, and now next week I have four reports that I'm going to be working with." (00:28:20): There just wasn't that much for the completely new manager who didn't have an MBA, wasn't on some sort of ladder, and just one day got dropped and asked to kind of go and support a couple people who were starting next week. I was brought back to that moment in time and realizing there really isn't that much that is great out there that is particularly geared for new managers, and I felt that I had to really learn and make a lot of these mistakes on my own, and even very fundamentally, I don't think that people ever really explained to me, what is a manager, what does it mean to do a good job as a manager of a handful of people. Right? (00:28:56): And so, it sparked this idea that this was something that was somewhat missing in the market, that there was an opportunity to just really write something that could speak to people like me and people, again, similar to me who maybe weren't on this ladder for 10 or 12 years, especially in tech, right, I knew many people who had gone through that. Then the second thing for me is I realized that I would likely also become a better manager through this process because it would force me to think about management a lot every single day. It would force me to reflect on my frameworks for management, and whenever you think about something all the time in the back of your head, it's just more top of mind. I was looking to become a better manager myself at that point, and that was the additional boost that I needed to commit to the project.
turns.zh:
谢谢。我曾梦想写一部伟大的美国小说。如今我依然想实现这个愿望。总有一天，我真想静下心来，写一部虚构作品。这件事一直萦绕在我的心头。我从未想过自己会写非虚构类书籍，更别说商业类书籍了。这些想法都是自然而然产生的。最初我写博客时，会把写给自己的信件发布到网上，有时出版商或相关人士会联系我，说：“你的这篇文章写得太棒了，有没有考虑把它改编成书？”很长一段时间，我都回答：“不行，因为我没信心把一个主题扩展成一部鸿篇巨制。我不认为自己是职业作家。”说实话，我确实找不到什么与众不同的独特视角。（00:27:03）我还觉得自己读的大多数书都需要大量研究，我当时就想：“我不喜欢研究，也不擅长这事。” 但有一天，出版商联系我，说：“你写的关于新晋管理者的建议，特别是在领导力方面的，似乎很能引起读者共鸣。我们想聊聊这个方向。”那次通话真的改变了我的视角，因为它让我发现了市场上缺失的独特视角。对吧？（00:27:44）再说，我写的大部分内容都是给自己的建议，但这让我回想起自己刚成为管理者时的情景。有一天，我去书店寻找管理相关的资源，却发现大多数书都是由执掌大企业多年的CEO写的，或者是管理顾问写的，根本不适用于那些“刚从IC晋升为manager，接下来一周就要带四个下属”的新手管理者。（00:28:20）市场上根本没有针对零基础新手管理者的优质资源。我意识到自己不得不靠自己摸索，犯很多错误，甚至连最基本的管理者定义、如何管理好团队这些问题都没人系统讲解。对吧？（00:28:56）于是，我萌生了填补市场空白的想法，写一本能帮助像我这样、甚至和我相似（没读过MBA、没走过晋升通道、突然接手新团队的人）的书。第二个启发是，我意识到自己可能也会成为管理者。
通过这个过程，我能成为一名更出色的管理者，因为它迫使我每天都深入思考管理问题。它促使我反思自己的管理框架，而当你不断在脑海中反复思考某件事时，它就会变得更加清晰易记。当时我正致力于提升自己的管理能力，而这正是我全身心投入这个项目所需的额外动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Has that last piece bitten you in the butt at all, when you maybe make a mistake as a manager and people are like, "Julie, you wrote this book on management. What the hell's going on?"
turns.zh: 最后那件事有没有让你觉得很糟糕？比如当你作为管理者犯了错，人们会说：“朱莉，你写了本管理学著作。到底怎么回事？”

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I always tell people, I tell my own reports as well, it's like, "You might come in and you might have read my book and you might think that somehow I am a really great manager and an expert in management, and I always try. I'm going to lower your expectations. I'm still learning." There's a lot of things that I'm still working on that I know I'm not perfect at, but that's what I think it is. Right? I think so much about, for me, at least, learning to be a better manager, and I know I'll probably be on this journey for the rest of my life is that you can know oftentimes the theory because the theory is it makes sense, right? It's like, okay, we all been in that situation. We can feel. It is so hard to just actually put it in practice. It's so hard to do some of these things every single day because they're sort of counterintuitive and it is so hard to apply it to the appropriate context. (00:30:30): Just even the example I gave earlier, managing early career, new grads is just completely different than managing really senior people and being able to tailor to each individual person or each specific group of people because humans are, we're all different. We're all unique. Right? No two people are the same. No groups of people are the same. So, it is an art as anything else. A lot of it too is about learning about who I am, what am I good at, what am I not good at, how can I be more honest and more authentic to my own strengths and weaknesses, and then be able to pair that up with the person that I'm talking to or the group of people that I'm working with. So, definitely not by any means today still consider myself great or an expert or whatnot. I think everyone else, I'm still trying to get better.
turns.zh: 我总是跟别人说——包括我手下的人——我会说：“你可能刚进公司，读过我的书，觉得我是个超级棒的管理者，是管理领域的专家。但我得提醒你，我还在学习中。” 还有很多东西我至今仍在努力改进，虽然我知道自己并非完美，但这就是现实，对吧？至少对我来说，学习如何成为一名更好的管理者至关重要。我知道这将是我一生的修行，因为你可能掌握了理论框架——理论听起来很合理，对吧？比如，‘我们都经历过那种情况，能感同身受’。但真正付诸实践却难上加难。每天践行这些理念尤其困难，因为它们往往违背直觉，还要根据具体情境灵活运用。（00:30:30） 就拿我之前提到的例子来说，管理初入职场的新人与管理资深员工完全不同。每个人的情况各不相同，人类本质上都是独特的个体。没有两个人是完全相同的，没有一群人是完全一样的。所以，这也是一门艺术。很多时候还需要深刻了解自己——自己擅长什么，不擅长什么，如何更诚实地展现自己的优缺点，然后根据交谈对象或合作团队进行调整。所以，我今天绝不认为自己已经很棒或是个专家了。我觉得其他人也会说，我还在努力进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a little bit how I feel where people think that I've got it all figured out, I'd be like the most amazing product manager they've ever worked with, and I feel like I could never get a regular job again, because the hype. The expectations would be way too high. People forget that I have time to think, research, process, and that kind of thing. And so, I can never get a PM job again. This is basically the problem that I've created for myself.
turns.zh: 这就是我的感受——人们总觉得我无所不知，觉得我是个他们共事过的最出色的产品经理，但我觉得自己再也找不到普通工作了，因为期望值太高了。人们忘了我有时间思考、研究、反思等等。所以，我再也找不到产品经理的工作了。这基本上是我自己给自己制造的难题。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I think you'd be a pretty great PM, Lenny.
turns.zh: 我觉得你会是个很棒的产品经理，伦尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's all an illusion, but I appreciate it. And then the other piece is that you pointed this out, that a lot of people don't realize when folks like us write, it's like us figuring it out. It's not like we have the answer and we're just like, "Okay, here, I'm just going to write down the answer I already have in my head." The process of writing is how we learn a lot about these sorts of things, and a lot of people don't realize that.
turns.zh: 这一切都是假象，但我很感激。另外，你指出了一个问题——很多人没有意识到，当我们这样的人写作时，其实是在不断摸索。不是说我们已经有现成的答案，然后就写下来。写作的过程本身就是学习的过程，而很多人没有意识到这一点。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah, I absolutely agree. Like I said, it's about reminding ourselves. Right? I always often say I'm the number one audience for my own writing because I'm the person who needs to really hear it the most.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全同意。就像我说的，关键在于提醒自己。对吧？我常说，我自己是自己作品的头号读者，因为我是最需要听到这些反馈的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how I feel a lot of times. When I go back to my own pieces, like, "Oh yeah. Okay. That's what I wanted to remember." On the writing, something I wanted to ask about is you've kind of slowed down for a good reason. You have a startup to run and you've started doing more tweeting than news lettering and blogging. How do you think about that? Just, is that intentional? How do you think about, I don't know, Twitter versus newsletters and other things?
turns.zh: 嗯，我很多时候都有这种感觉。当我回看自己写的文章时，会想：“哦，对了。原来这就是我想记住的东西。” 关于写作，我想问一下，你最近放慢了写作节奏，这是有充分理由的。你要经营一家初创公司，而且现在发推特比发通讯和写博客更频繁。你怎么看待这一点？这是刻意为之吗？你如何看待推特与通讯、其他形式的写作相比？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah, it was very much. This is another New Year's resolution that came up later. Right? One of the things that I recognize about myself is I kind of have a tendency to ramble, and I've gotten this feedback as well in 360s where I'm not always the clearest communicator. I can be a pretty good storyteller and I am clearer in writing often than I am in person, but this was another area that I wanted to get better at. Right? I wanted to get better at in the moment communicating more clearly and being just a little bit sharper, a little bit crisper in the points that I had to make. (00:32:56): I remember I work with a number of colleagues who are just so good at this. Right? There will be some really complex topic, this big product thing that we're trying to figure out, and in the moment, they would go and they would say, "Okay, I see. This is what the problem is. The problem is one, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, two, blah, blah, blah, three. Right?" Everybody like, "Yeah, that's amazing. That's so crystal clear." This huge thing we're all talking past each other there now became boiled to something so sharp and so beautiful. Right? I always had so much respect and admiration for the people who could do that, and that wasn't me, but I was like, "Okay, well, as anything, if I have a thing I like and want and admire and respect, I could at least get better at it. Maybe I'll never be at that level, but I can work towards it." (00:33:36): And one of the ways I saw of working towards that is, well, let's just change it up. I'd been doing long-form, which again, works really well for these stories and this kind of more meandering prose, but what if I just push myself to communicate in a much shorter form which is going to force me to really strip away all that ornamentation and focus on the core idea. And I was like, "I'm just going to go and publish threads on Twitter for a year." Again, same thing. Write once a week a little thread and just take whatever is the advice I needed to give myself and then boil that down to a tweet form. So, also, it has helped me. It has helped me to get better at enumerating things. I think more naturally now sometimes. It's like 1, 2, 3, and that has helped me as well in just, again, the day job and the way that I communicate. Still a long ways to go. But I think Twitter is really great at that. It's really great at trying to boil it down to the essence of what it is that one wants to communicate.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。这是后来才有的新年决心，对吧？我发现自己有倾向于东拉西扯的毛病，360度评估反馈中也提到过，我不总是表达得很清晰。我讲故事的能力还不错，写作时也比口头更清晰，但这也是我想改进的领域。对吧？我想提高即时清晰表达的能力，让我想传达的观点更简洁明了。（00:32:56）：我记得和一些同事合作，他们在这方面做得很好。比如，面对一个复杂的产品问题，我们要共同攻克，现场他们会说：“好的，我明白了。问题在于第一，第二，第三。” 每个人都会惊叹：“哇，太棒了！太清晰了！” 原本大家各说各话的复杂问题，突然被提炼得简洁明了。对吧？我一直很敬佩能做到这样的人，虽然我做不到，但我想：好吧，只要喜欢、渴望、钦佩并尊重某种技能，我至少应该努力去提升。也许达不到那个水平，但可以朝着它努力。（00:33:36）：我找到的一个方法就是改变现状。我一直写长篇文章，这对讲述故事和更随意的散文来说效果很好，但如果我强迫自己用更简短的形式交流，就必须去掉所有装饰，专注于核心观点。我就想：“那我就去推特上发一年推文。” 同样，每周写一篇短文，把我想给自己的建议提炼成推文。这对我也有帮助。它让我更擅长列举要点。我现在思考问题时更自然了。比如1、2、3，这样做对我的日常工作和沟通方式也有帮助。不过要走的路还很长。但我觉得推特在这方面确实很棒，它能帮助你把想传达的信息提炼到最本质的东西上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you use these tools to help work on a very specific skill that you're hoping to develop. So, you said that worked. Is that something you'd recommend to folks that are working on something like this and have a challenge there too?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你用这些工具来提升自己希望发展的特定技能。所以你说这方法有效。对于那些在类似领域遇到挑战的人，你会推荐这样做吗？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I do. I talk to a lot of people who want to write more because they feel like there is a lot of benefits, and maybe it's because writers often talk about all of the benefits, but a lot of people do maybe find it, as you were saying earlier, hard to get started. Right? My number one advice is try to find an angle that's going to work for you because if you find yourself writing for your audience, if you find yourself writing because you want likes or you want a certain number of views, that actually is a really hard barrier to overcome because you don't have control over all of that. But if you write because you're trying to work on a particular key skill, whether it is clarity of thinking, whether it's helping you work through some stuff that's complicated in your mind, whether it's just, again, working on being more comfortable, putting your voice out there, then make it a goal, but make it a action goal. Make it like a word count goal. (00:35:26): I saw this on Twitter, I think it was that last year, the idea of the 30 days of just writing a thing every day or tweeting a thing every day. Right? You see this in design too. There's Inktober which is you just draw a thing every single day in the month of October, and I love those types of structures and programs. I think that they're a way to go and get into the habit of that. Everyone kind of feels like they can do anything for 30 days. You can do anything for three months if you just commit to doing it once a week. It doesn't have to be forever. It doesn't have to be some sort of like five-year thing and the commitment. That's a huge milestone. You just have to do it for a little bit and then reflect on it. Is it really helping you? Is it actually helping you get closer to that goal? And that's usually the easiest way I've found to get started.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实这么认为。我接触过很多想多写作的人，他们觉得写作有很多好处，或许正是因为作家们总在强调这些好处，但很多人确实会像你之前说的，觉得很难开始写作。对吧？我的首要建议是，试着找到适合自己的写作方向。如果你为了迎合读者而写作，如果你写作只是为了获得点赞或点击量，那这其实是个很难克服的障碍，因为这些东西你无法完全掌控。但如果你写作是为了磨练某项关键技能——无论是提升思维清晰度，还是理清脑海中的复杂思路，又或者是增强自信、勇于表达——那就把它设定为一个目标，但要把它转化为行动目标。比如设定一个字数目标。（00:35:26）我在推特上看到过这样一个想法，去年有人提倡每天写一篇文章或发一条推文，持续30天。这种结构化的挑战在其他领域也很常见，比如“墨水十月”活动——10月份每天画一幅画。我特别喜欢这种模式和挑战机制。它们能帮助人养成习惯。很多人觉得自己能坚持30天，但其实每周写一次、持续三个月也足够了。不必追求永久坚持，也不必定下五年的宏伟计划。只要先坚持一段时间，再反思效果如何——这才是最容易入门的办法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Just creating a little bit of structure for yourself so you don't have to think about it, you just do it, and I don't care what I do on that day, but I'm doing it, and maybe one time something will come out really great. (00:36:16): This episode is brought to you by Sprig. If you've been a member of my community for a while, you know I'm a user, fan, and investor in Sprig. Sprig is a user research platform that makes getting user insights from your product as easy and fast as getting analytics. The best product and research teams at companies like Loom, Opendoor, and Dropbox use Sprig's in-product surveys to target specific users, start collecting insights, and identify issues and opportunities related to activation onboarding engagement and more. Talk about a platform that pays for itself. (00:36:48): But I'm perhaps most excited about Sprig's newest launch which extends the power of the platform prelaunch and makes it possible to test mockups and prototypes with your own users in minutes. The testing interface is super slick and doesn't require any of the typical plugins that make testing with your own users unappealing, and with unlimited seats, you're able to invite anyone from your company to view and use insights generated by Sprig. If you want to get started, head over to sprig.com/lenny and mention that I sent you. (00:37:18): That reminds me of something I wanted to plus-one, the point that especially on Twitter, I find whenever you're trying to go viral, it just comes across often is just like, okay, they're just trying to go viral. So lame. This person just wants a lot of likes versus I just want to share a thing that's interesting to me quickly, or here's how I want to think about it, or here's just a thing I want to remember in the future. I find those end up being a lot more successful.
turns.zh:
我特别喜欢这样做。就是为自己设定一点结构，这样你就不必去想太多，只需按部就班地去做。其实我并不在乎那天自己做了什么，但只要行动起来，说不定就能创作出非常棒的成果。（00:36:16）本期节目由Sprig赞助。如果你已经关注我的社区有一段时间了，就会知道我既是Sprig的用户、粉丝，也是投资人。Sprig是一个用户研究平台，能像获取分析数据一样轻松快速地从产品中获取用户洞察。Loom、Opendoor和Dropbox等公司的顶尖产品和研究团队都在使用Sprig的内置调查功能，精准定位特定用户，收集洞察，识别与激活、用户留存等相关的问题和机遇。这真是一个物超所值的平台。

（00:36:48）但我最兴奋的可能是Sprig最新推出的功能，它将平台的强大功能延伸至产品发布前，能让你在几分钟内就与自己的用户测试原型和模型。测试界面非常流畅，无需任何传统插件（那些插件往往让用户测试体验大打折扣），而且拥有无限席位，你可以邀请公司内任何人查看和使用Sprig生成的洞察。如果你想开始使用，可以访问sprig.com/lenny，并提及我是推荐你来的。

（00:37:18）这让我想起我想点赞的一个观点：尤其是在Twitter上，我发现每当你试图走红时，人们往往会觉得你只是为了出名。这太无趣了。有些人只是想获得大量点赞，而我只想快速分享对我有趣的内容，或者记录下未来的思考要点。我发现这些内容往往更受欢迎。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: That's right. Yeah, that's totally right. I think it's what really gets you interested in it is likely the thread that you want to enroll and to continue to explore. If you're just try and say what you think people want to hear, it just comes across not that genuine, and personally, not that interesting.
turns.zh: 没错。是的，这完全正确。我认为真正能激发你兴趣的，很可能是你想参与并继续探索的线程。如果你只是试图说出人们想听的话，就会显得不真诚，而且个人而言，也没那么有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the thing I've kind of learned is if I find something interesting, other people will find it interesting, and so, I'll just share that in some form and often ends up being really helpful to a lot of people. Speaking of Twitter, one of the threads I've liked best that you've written about, and I think you've done this a couple times, is around product thinking and product sense and how to build that muscle. And so, I'd love to just hear your advice on for folks that are thinking about how do I get better at product sense and product thinking. What are ways that people can get better at these things?
turns.zh: 是的，我学到的一点是，如果我觉得某件事有趣，其他人也会觉得有趣。所以，我会以某种形式分享出来，通常这对很多人都非常有帮助。说到Twitter，你写过的最让我喜欢的帖子之一（我觉得你已经写过好几次了）是关于产品思维和产品敏锐度，以及如何培养这些能力的。所以，我很想听听你对那些想提高产品敏锐度和产品思维能力的人的建议。人们可以通过哪些方法来提高这些能力呢？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: The number one advice that I always have for people when talking about product sensor or product thinking is it's just really about observation and it's about curiosity and can start by first observing yourself. Every time you're going to go and use something, every time you're going to have a new experience, you download an app, you try something new, it's take the moment to reflect on your emotion or your assumption at every step. Right? What was the new user experience? At what moment did it become clear to you what was going on? When were you confused? How many times did you tap something and then had to exit because you went down a wrong pathway? And even before that, it's like what even led you to trying this service in the first place to downloading the app? Was it word of mouth? Did you see something on the internet? Did somebody that you respect pitch it? (00:39:07): But these are all ways in which we're learning about how things work, how products work. It always starts by just if you first observe yourself, then you'll make a lot of progress. Right? And oftentimes it's hard to do that because sometimes we're just, we're going through the motions or we're not necessarily sitting down and analyzing every step of it. But the first step I think is just to get really good, comfortable, familiar, habitual with just that personal observation. (00:39:31): The second step is then, okay, cool, you do that for yourself. Well, that's not enough because you're not the world. Right? You don't necessarily represent everyone, but now it's to just build on those circles. So, the next thing you do is you go and actually observe and share those observations with somebody else, and so, how that often looks is discussions about products. So, you download this, why did you download this? What made you decide that this was a great app? Do you think it's a great app? What was compelling about it? And to just really find the curiosity of thinking through which decisions did the builders or the creators of something make and what was the impact of it on us users, us customers and so forth. (00:40:07): So, often it goes into then the next step which is spending a lot of time sharing those observations and critiquing. Right? I mean, our role of thumb is really I want to get better. How often are you having a conversation with somebody about products, dissecting something, and really, what did you think was good or bad about it, and engaging that because if you aren't, it's going to be harder for you to actually learn about all of those different micro decision and what its impact is. (00:40:33): And then you can go a little broader than that. Right? There's lots of really great resources. There's amazing folks on the internet who will go down and really dissect... I love Eugene Wei's writing. I love Kevin Kwak. I always learn something because they take these apps like Figma or TikTok or whatever it is, and then they really go very, very deep with their own observations, what works, what patterns do we see across different apps that are successful and that aren't. Right? And this is all helping us to understand what are these again, the key decisions and what impact does it lead to that helps us become better at then making those intentional decisions in the product. So, that's a huge part of it. (00:41:13): I think another thing then is of course you have to try and validate. So, one thing we can do is of course we look at opinions, we look at reactions. That's data. Right? That's the qualitative side. I think the other side is quantitative. So often if you are building products and you have the opportunity to run experiments, to do AB tests, or if you're working on one team but lots of other people in lots of other teams are also doing AB tests, it's so interesting to then be able to ask people, ask the product manager on the other team about what they're learning about their products, and to really be able to look at specific decisions and what causally happened as a result. (00:41:48): That's what I love about AB tests, and I think being really deep in the data and really going back to can we infer some sort of causal relationship because we're... Correlation or causation, but with causation with AB tests, can we actually pick up some of these learnings, can we look at patterns, and can we take some insights away that helps validate and confirm a lot of the hypotheses that we had about product, and just ingesting as much of that as you can also helps develop your instinct for what works and what doesn't. Right? (00:42:17): I always find people often have this, oh, design and user experience is on the other side of the coin. It's like it's a totally different industry, and they're at odds with each other, being data informed and being quantitative versus being very designer-y and subjective and caring about those aesthetics. I just think that's totally wrong. I think that there really... One helps confirm the assumptions or the other. Right? No, it is true that looking at a bunch of numbers isn't often going to tell you exactly the leaps of faith that you need to make to start something new, but they surely can help you validate whether a number of your assumptions about how people work or the way the world works are true or not. (00:42:57): And so, I know of a lot of really brilliant product thinkers who got that way not necessarily because they came through the route of subjective observation, but because they went and they were so disciplined about always studying what happened, what was the impact in the numbers and people and so forth, and then eventually you marry that of course with, well, why might that be the case, and you get into the qualitative side and the observation, but these two both support each other in helping to build a really great product sense.
turns.zh:
关于产品感知或产品思维，我给人们的首要建议就是：这其实只关乎观察与好奇心。你可以从观察自己开始。每次你要使用某个产品、体验新事物、下载应用或尝试新事物时，都应该停下来反思每个步骤中的情绪或假设。比如：新用户体验是怎样的？在哪个瞬间你才意识到问题的所在？什么时候感到困惑？有多少次因为误入歧途而不得不退出？甚至在此之前，究竟是什么促使你最初尝试这项服务、下载应用？是口口相传？还是在网上看到推荐？又或者是受尊敬的人推荐的？  

（00:39:07）但这些都是我们了解产品运作方式的途径。首先要观察自己，这样才能取得长足进步。是吧？但很多时候我们很难做到这一点——要么机械操作，要么不愿停下来分析每个步骤。但第一步就是要养成观察自我的习惯。  

（00:39:31）第二步是，将这种自我观察延伸到他人。毕竟，你不能代表全世界。但你可以通过不断拓展圈子来深化理解。比如，与他人讨论产品体验：你为何下载这款应用？是什么让你认定它很棒？你认为它真的优秀吗？其中的关键点在于，探究产品创作者的决策及其对用户的影响。  

（00:40:07）接下来，就是通过分享观察与批判来深化理解。比如与人探讨产品，剖析其优劣，并积极参与其中。若不这样做，就很难真正理解微观决策及其影响。  

（00:40:33）最后，可以更广泛地探索优质资源。比如尤金·韦（Eugene Wei）和郭凯文（Kevin Kwak）的文章，他们深入剖析Figma、TikTok等应用，揭示成功与失败的共性模式。这些都帮助我们理解关键决策及其影响，从而提升产品决策能力。这是关键所在。  

（00:41:13）验证观点同样重要。我们可以通过收集用户反馈和数据来验证假设，但定性分析与定量分析同样重要。
通常来说，如果你正在开发产品，并且有机会进行实验、开展AB测试，或者如果你在一个团队中工作，而其他许多团队也在进行AB测试，那么能够向其他团队的产品经理询问他们对产品的洞察，并真正审视具体决策及其因果关系，这会非常有趣。（00:41:48）：这就是我热爱AB测试的原因。我认为深入研究数据，追溯因果关系至关重要——因为我们要区分相关性和因果性。在AB测试中，我们能否发现因果关系？能否发现规律？能否从中获取见解，验证和确认我们对产品的诸多假设？尽可能多地吸收这些信息，也有助于培养你对什么有效、什么无效的直觉。对吧？（00:42:17）：我发现很多人常有这样的误区，认为设计和用户体验是截然不同的。他们认为这两个领域完全不相容，数据驱动和量化思维与注重美学和主观判断的设计思维水火不容。我认为这种观点大错特错。我认为两者实际上是相辅相成的。对吧？没错，光看一堆数据通常无法让你获得推陈出新所需的信心，但它们肯定能帮助你验证你对用户行为或世界运行规律的诸多假设是否正确。（00:42:57）：我认识很多极其出色的产品思考者，他们之所以能取得成功，不一定是因为他们善于进行主观观察，而是因为他们始终坚持研究实际发生了什么，数据和用户反馈带来了什么影响等。最终，你会将这些分析与因果推理相结合，进而开展定性研究和观察。但这两者相辅相成，有助于培养卓越的产品洞察力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. There's so much material there that we could go on and on. On that last point, I wanted to kind of double-click on it a little bit. So, say you're founder and you're like, "Man, I have all these really clear vision and ideas of where I want to go with my product," and your team's like, "Oh, I don't know if this is right. What if we do a little more user research or run some experiments?" Do you have any advice to the founder of just when to rely on their gut and experience and just go with that versus doing more research, getting more data?
turns.zh: 太棒了。里面有太多内容了，我们可以聊个没完没了。关于最后一点，我想再深入探讨一下。假设你是一位创始人，你满怀热情地说：“天啊，我对产品的发展方向有非常清晰的愿景和构想！”但团队却说：“哦，我不确定这是否正确。不如先做些用户调研或者开展实验试试？”对于创始人来说，何时应该相信自己的直觉和经验、坚定执行，何时又需要通过更多调研获取数据，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: That is a really great question. One of the most common pieces of advice for founders, and I actually also had to remind myself constantly of this one is the more you know your customers, the more you can really close your eyes and just imagine everything about their life and what they're doing on almost like a minute to minute basis, probably the better you're going to do in terms of coming up with something that's going to meaningfully solve a problem for them. Right? (00:44:15): And so, that comes from a couple of different places. The first is, look, if you're the person you're building for, you're the target audience, awesome. You probably do have a lot of stuff that is instinctively known to you, and maybe in those cases, your team doesn't have that experience and they maybe can't feel the same level of conviction you do, and they might be asking you, ""Hey, well, can we validate?" and all of that. Right? It's always good advice, but sometimes, you're so deep in it and you can... You're this person or you know this person, or you did this job that probably can trust your instincts and your gut quite a bit. (00:44:48): I remember early days at Facebook, that was us. Everybody who worked at the company was either a college dropout or a recent college grad, and we were building a product for college students. I mean, we were the perfect... It was like for us by us. We understood exactly what this audience wanted. If we didn't, we would call up some friends. I mean, this was just pure target a demographic for what we were building. (00:45:10): But eventually if that's not true, and it evolved at Facebook, and it evolves for companies. You might start out that way, but eventually, we started to open up to the world. We started to add people in different countries. The percentage of people that were college grads who were like us who were using the product started to shrink, became a smaller and smaller percentage of actually all core Facebook users, so therefore our intuitions started to become less and less reliable. I remember in spectacular fashion, I think this was in 2008 or '09, we had a string of failures, big kind of launches that were failures, and I think it was because we reached the end of our intuition for the user base at that particular moment. (00:45:49): That's true for founders as well. Sometimes you're building a product in a domain where you weren't the target audience. Right? I feel this right now for myself. I'm building an analytics product. I was never a data analyst. I understand the outside, the value of data, but I never did the job, and therefore, what I really needed to do was just spend a lot of time with data scientists immersing or actually just trying to do the job myself because the better that I understand what it is and what it's like and what the company context is, and I think with, for SaaS companies in particular, you might have done the job at one company, but you probably didn't do it at 20 or 50 companies, and you're probably selling to a lot of companies so it's just way more critical for you to spend a lot of time interviewing customers because your intuition is likely not going to carry you nearly as far as if you're building, again, a very consumer product for a very consumer audience of which you yourself are part of. (00:46:41): So, I do think that, yeah, it doesn't matter that you need to really understand your customers. Do you have to go out and do the work, have the conversations, teach yourself the things that they do? It depends a bit on the context, depends on where you are, but it's never bad advice. The better you understand your customers, I think the better you're going to be able to build a product.
turns.zh:
这确实是个很棒的问题。对于创业者来说，最常见的建议之一——我自己也经常需要时刻提醒自己——就是：你对客户了解得越多，就越能闭上眼睛，想象他们生活的方方面面，甚至是他们每分每秒在做的事。这样一来，你就更有可能开发出真正能为他们解决问题的创新方案。对吧？（00:44:15）  

这源于几个方面。首先，如果你就是你所服务的目标客户，那当然再好不过了。你很可能对很多事情有着本能的理解，而在这种情况下，你的团队可能没有这样的经验，无法达到你同样的信念水平，他们可能会问你：“嘿，我们能验证一下吗？”之类的问题。对吧？这永远是个好建议，但有时你深陷其中太久，可能……你自己就是这个人，或者你认识这个人，或者你做过这份工作，因此可以相当信任自己的直觉和本能。（00:44:48）  

我记得Facebook早期，我们就是这样的。公司里的每个人要么是大学辍学生，要么是刚毕业的大学生，而我们开发的产品是面向大学生的。可以说，我们是为自己而做的，完全理解目标用户的需求。如果不了解，我们就会去找朋友咨询。我们的产品定位就是精准针对这个群体。（00:45:10）  

但最终，如果这种情况不再成立，Facebook和其他公司一样也在不断发展。你可能一开始是这样，但最终我们开始向外开放，吸纳不同国家的人才。像我们这样使用产品的大学毕业生比例开始下降，在Facebook所有核心用户中所占比例越来越小，因此我们的直觉越来越不可靠。我记得2008或2009年，我们接连遭遇失败，推出的重大产品都以失败告终，原因就是我们在那一刻已经用尽了对用户群体的直觉理解。（00:45:49）  

对于创业者来说也是如此。有时你开发的产品所在领域并非你的目标客户群体。对吧？我现在自己就深有体会。我正在开发一个分析产品，但我从未做过数据分析师。我了解数据的外部价值，但从未亲自从事过这份工作。因此，我真正需要做的，就是花大量时间与数据科学家交流，甚至亲自尝试这份工作，因为这样我才能更深入理解其本质、公司背景。特别是对于SaaS公司而言，你可能在一家公司做过这份工作，但在20或50家公司未必做过，因此花大量时间采访客户对你是至关重要的，因为你的直觉很可能无法像为消费者群体开发产品时那样有效。（00:46:41）  

所以，我确实认为，你确实需要真正了解你的客户。是否需要亲自去实地考察、交流、自学他们的行为？这取决于具体情况和所处阶段。
但这绝不是一条糟糕的建议。我认为，你对客户的了解越透彻，就越能成功打造出优质的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that advice of just this model of the more time the founder spends with their customers, the more you can trust that they're going to have the right sorts of instincts, and the less they start to spend time there, maybe start running more experiments and doing more research as a team around the founder. That's interesting.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个模型的建议——创始人与客户相处的时间越多，你就越能相信他们会具备正确的直觉；而当他们花在客户身上的时间越少时，团队或许就需要更多地开展实验和研究。这点挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah. Or the larger your user base becomes, the less reliable any one or 10 or even a hundred people are in terms of understanding the whole. Right? It's just the numbers get too big.
turns.zh: 是啊，或者说当你的用户群规模越大时，单个用户、十个用户甚至一百个用户对整体情况的理解就越不可靠了。对吧？因为用户数量实在太大了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And luckily in theory, you have a lot more data at that point, and so, you can actually run experiments and start relying on data.
turns.zh: 幸运的是，从理论上讲，这时你能获取更多数据，因此可以开展实验并开始依赖数据。

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: That's right, yeah.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I also wanted to get your advice on. It's something that a lot of founders, especially, and even PMs come to me around is product review meetings and designer meetings, and I know you've run many, and so, I wanted to get your thoughts of just how should companies structure product review meetings or designer meetings, who should be in the room, how should they be set up. Any advice for folks that are trying to figure that out?
turns.zh: 还有个问题想请教您。很多创始人，尤其是产品经理，都会向我咨询产品评审会和设计师会议的事宜。我知道您参加过很多这样的会议，所以想听听您的看法：公司应该如何组织产品评审会或设计师会议？会议应该有哪些人员参与？又该如何安排流程？对于那些正在探索这方面的人，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I really believe that it's never a bad thing, it's always a better thing to have more feedback. Right? And so, often, I think you don't necessarily want to be like, "Oh, we have the one review meeting and that's the one in which we get everyone's opinions out and we make all these decisions, and then we're done." I think about product and feedback as just the more, the better. Right? And most people, again, everyone, especially with design, has an opinion to some degree, and so, all opinions are valid because they are a true opinion. The question is how do you then prioritize, how do you figure out what it is that you should do because we also can't... It isn't successful to try and do things by consensus. You're never going to get a group of people, smart people to agree about what is absolutely the best design. (00:48:32): So, one principle is, okay, great. If you're going to have feedback on the product, more is better. Try and have different sessions with different groups of people. I would advise a designer, "Hey, go in, actually do a critique with a design audience, but go and then show this to the people who are most directly working on the product because they're going to have a different set of knowledge, but then go and see if you can find some people outside of your direct team who don't have as much bias on just knowing exactly how things work and then show them the user experience, and then go and actually see if you can find a group of target customers for who we're actually going to launch, and then run some user research sessions and get feedback. "They all are going to be valuable. They all might contradict each other to some degree, but the right answer isn't because we don't like disagreement, let's just go with one and then ignore the others. Everyone is going to have something to contribute to the product because everyone has that different perspective. (00:49:24): So, again, lots of sessions, lots of user review sessions, awesome. Okay, but then there is an important job which is the synthesis of all of that feedback and a way of understanding what really matters. The way that I often think about this is we have to be absolutely clear on who is that target audience and what is the most important problem that we're trying to solve for them. Right? So, if you can get every group to align on this is who it is. Again, go and paint that very clear picture of the person, the problem, what it is that we're trying to help them with, and then what is most important. What is the job? I really love the jobs to be done for it, but what's the job that this particular feature or product is going to fulfill for that person? (00:50:08): Then it makes it easier for us to then start to categorize different buckets of feedback because the first thing that's most important to address is, well, is this thing actually valuable, is this solving the problem?, is it doing the job correctly, and if a lot of other stuff below is bad, but this is good, then we can move on to kind of the next most important thing. But if all the other stuff is maybe even good or interesting, but this is not there, then we should just actually disregard all the other stuff until we are quite certain that we've gotten the core value, we understand the user, this in some sense is addressing the core pain. (00:50:45): And then once we do that, then let's focus on the next layer which I think about as ease of use. Right? So, okay, cool. We've figured out that we validated, this thing is valuable. It does solve the job. Now, is it easy to use? Are people confused? Are they getting hung up somewhere? Is it just really slow, so no one can use it because it just takes 10 seconds to load each time? Ease of use is just about can people access the value in a really great manner. That's the next most important bucket. (00:51:11): And then finally, if it is valuable, it's easy to use, then I think we get into is it joyful to use, is it pleasurable, does it really exceed expectations, and I think that is the bar that we should aim for whenever we are creating products. Here, you might have debates about colors, or aesthetic properties, or animation and delight, and all of the other things that just make it that much more enjoyable and surprising and wonderful for the core audience. But you don't want to just focus on that and then lose, okay, actually, this thing wasn't valuable and it loaded in 10 seconds. Who cares about how great was the animation when the thing doesn't even load? So, I think there's a work to do to try and actually help the different pieces of feedback get synthesized so we understand what bucket they are and we can have the right order of prioritization to make sure we tackle the most important things first.
turns.zh:
我真的认为，多听取反馈永远是件好事，而不是坏事。对吧？所以，我通常不赞成那种"我们只开一次评审会，让大家畅谈想法，然后就拍板决定"的做法。我认为产品和反馈越多越好，对吧？大多数人，尤其是设计师，总会有自己的看法。毕竟，每个人的意见都是有价值的，因为那是真实的想法。关键在于如何筛选并确定优先级，毕竟靠共识来决策是行不通的。你永远无法让一群聪明的人就最佳设计达成一致。（00:48:32）所以，基本原则是：如果要收集产品反馈，越多越好。尝试与不同群体开展不同形式的评审会。我建议设计师这样做：首先与设计师团队进行评审，然后向直接参与产品开发的人员展示设计成果，因为他们对产品有更深入的了解。接着，再找一些不受产品固有知识局限的目标用户群体进行测试，最后开展用户研究获取反馈。所有这些反馈都很有价值，即便存在不同意见，也不应简单否定某个观点而忽视其他声音。每个人都能为产品带来独特视角。（00:49:24）所以，多次开展用户评审非常重要。但关键在于如何整合所有反馈，理解其核心价值。我常认为，要明确目标用户是谁，解决的最核心问题是什么。确保每个团队都能围绕这些核心要素达成共识。比如，先清晰勾勒用户画像、问题场景、产品价值主张，再明确产品最核心的功能——即解决用户的哪些关键痛点。（00:50:08）这样就能更高效地分类反馈：首要评估产品价值、解决问题的能力。如果其他功能虽有不足，但核心功能优秀，那么可以转向下一个优先级。但若其他功能尚可或有趣，但核心功能缺失，那就应暂缓其他讨论，直到确定核心价值、理解用户需求、精准解决痛点为止。（00:50:45）确认核心价值后，再关注易用性等次要维度。
困惑了？他们是卡在某个地方了吗？还是说速度实在太慢，每次加载要10秒钟，导致没人能用？易用性关键在于用户能否顺畅获取价值。这是第二重要维度。（00:51:11）最后，如果产品有价值且易用，那用户使用时是否会感到愉悦？是否能超出预期？我认为这才是我们设计产品时应当追求的标准。在这里，可能会有关于颜色、美学属性、动画效果和趣味性的讨论，所有这些元素都能为核心用户带来更愉快的体验。但切不可只专注于这些表象层面，而忽视了产品核心价值——比如加载速度太慢。动画再出色，加载速度太慢用户也无感。所以，我们需要努力整合各种反馈，准确判断其归属维度，并合理分配优先级，确保最重要的问题能得到优先解决。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to be clear, this is a kind of ongoing process. This isn't one meeting where you go through all these four layers. Right?
turns.zh: 需要说明的是，这个过程是持续进行的。这不是一次性开会就能完成所有四个层级分析的。对吧？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And then is your advice to focus on it in that sequence generally and not focus on say the delight and so you make it through these other points, or do you find it's helpful to think about all these things at once?
turns.zh: 好的。那么你的建议是，通常应该按顺序关注这些层级，而不是一股脑地先关注愉悦性，再逐步处理其他层级？还是说同时考虑所有因素会更有帮助？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
turns.en: I usually find that if you're going to go in and run a design critique or review session, it's helpful to start off front by saying, "Here's where we are in the process. This is the most important set of things we want to validate. We want to validate whether this actually solves the problem. We've validated it solves the problem, but now we validate whether it's easy to use," or something along those effect. So, being more specific about where you are, what kind of feedback matters the most at that particular phase for the team is valuable because if you don't do that, sometimes you'll just get all sorts of feedback, and some of it is you're not even ready for. The team's not even thinking about some of these additional level details or just thinking about the core stuff, and usually it follows just from how product development happens. (00:53:07): The first thing that often teams will come up with when they build a product is some kind of product brief or some kind of understanding of the user in a very high-level picture about how the product is. Usually, there's not high-fidelity mocks or prototypes at that stage. Right? And so, that's great because we're using a different fidelity. We're looking at documents and words and values and data as a way to understand the opportunity and that lends itself well to that kind of feedback. (00:53:35): But where I find that things get a little confusing is sometimes you will go and just make a prototype, and again, the goal of the prototype is to give a feeling of how it works. It's not that the team had already spent a bunch of time on the exact UI decisions or so forth, and so, what happens though is sometimes the audience or the people who are giving feedback, they can't always distinguish that. So, then the feedback goes immediately towards, "Oh, I don't like that shade of blue, or maybe we should put step two before step three," and that's not actually where the conversation is because we haven't actually gone and have conviction in just the first core piece of whether this is even the right thing to build or whether it really is solving an important enough problem. So, being very clear about where you are and what is the feedback that you want to get is important. (00:54:20): Now, again, eventually you go and you put stuff in front of customers. It's a little harder for them to just fully be able to distinguish between wait, what's the difference between the feedback versus around value versus ease of use. It gets all blended for them at that point in time though, so they'll just give whatever feedback. And again, I think that's fine. Just collect it, but then when you go and do the synthesis, when you go and do the prioritization, make sure that you're getting what you need at that stage.
turns.zh:
我通常发现，如果要参加设计评审或审查会议，最好先开门见山地说：“我们目前处于这个阶段。这是我们最需要验证的核心要素。我们已经确认了产品是否能解决问题，但现在要验证它是否易于使用。”或者类似的思路。所以，要明确当前所处的阶段，告诉团队在当前阶段最重要的反馈是什么，这很有价值。因为如果不这样做，有时会收到各种不着边际的反馈，有些甚至超出了团队的预期。团队可能还未考虑到某些更深层次的细节，只专注于核心功能，而这通常源于产品开发的流程特性。
（00:53:07）：团队在开发产品时，最先想到的通常是产品简介或对用户的高层次理解，了解产品的整体框架。此时通常没有高保真模型或原型。对吧？这很好，因为我们可以用不同的方式获取信息——通过文档、文字、价值观和数据来理解机会，这类反馈也很有效。
（00:53:35）：但我发现有时会遇到混淆的情况。比如团队刚制作了原型，目标是让用户感受产品运作方式，但团队其实还没深入研究具体的UI设计细节。此时，反馈者可能无法区分两者——他们会直接给出“我不喜欢那个蓝色调”或者“步骤二应该放在步骤三之前”之类的意见，而这其实不是关键讨论点，因为我们尚未确认是否要开发这个产品，或者它是否真正解决了重要问题。因此，明确当前阶段的目标以及希望获得的反馈至关重要。
（00:54:20）：最后，当产品面向客户时，他们更难区分不同层级的反馈——比如价值主张、易用性等。反馈会混为一谈，所以收集反馈固然重要，但在总结和优先级排序时，要确保收集到当前阶段真正需要的信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a colleague of the designer, say you're a PM or an engineer, data scientist or whatever, do you have any advice for just giving feedback to a designer in the critique?
turns.zh: 作为设计师的同事，比如产品经理、工程师、数据科学家等，你对在评审中给设计师反馈有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Julie Zhuo
